Introduction & Executive Summary** ### **1.1 Introduction** The key development since our previous forecast (released on 4th August) has been a rapidly deteriorating sovereign debt crisis in Europe, and to a lesser extent the United States. This along with renewed strains in financial markets subsequently triggered panic selling in the global equity and commodity markets across the board. Over the same period, gold prices have been tremendously volatile and the metal has traded within an enormous range of between $1,598 and $1,897/oz (basis London fix). Indeed, while the worsening macroeconomic environment led to a notable increase in safe haven purchases, gold was not immune to the above substantial liquidations; there is much evidence of large scale selling by commodity and hedge funds of gold positions in the over-the-counter and futures markets in late September and October. Importantly, though, a significant share of these sales seemed to have been “forced”, resulting from funds facing redemptions or investors’ urgent need to raise cash through selling liquid assets, such as gold. Further downward pressure on gold came from renewed fears over the banking sector which led to a squeeze on liquidity (an important financing source of commodity trading). In contrast, investor interest in physical bullion, particularly in Europe, surged to near all-time-highs in the third quarter, highlighting growing demand for gold as a means of wealth preservation. In the short term, our price forecast remains broadly similar under all three scenarios. With the debt crisis intensifying in Italy and Greece at the moment due to the ongoing failure to agree austerity plans, growing safe haven purchases should provide support for the gold price over the rest of 2011. However, if financial conditions continue to deteriorate, pushing us towards a deflationary environment, we would not rule out another major bout of selling in the market. But the downside for gold will be arrested by ongoing robust purchases from the official sector as well as strong physical buying in the key Asian markets, especially in India and China where demand jumped after prices slumped in late September. Looking further ahead, how the present crisis in the euro area develops will be of critical importance to the trend in investment demand and the gold price between 2012 and 2014. ### **1.2 The Base Case Scenario** 

**Mine production** is forecast to rise throughout the forecast period, with volumes growing by almost 300 tonnes over the next three years to reach 3,110 tonnes by 2014.  As with the previous report, the main driver for this increase is the strength of the project pipeline. Meanwhile, buoyant gold prices in 2012 and 2013 will also encourage the redevelopment of historic mines as well as boost increases in small-scale and informal mining.  Although the price is forecast to fall heavily in 2014, further, albeit modest, gains are expected that year as miners follow through with their growth plans. Since the last report, we have raised our forecast, reflecting a re-evaluation of informal and small-scale mining as well as a more bullish assessment of the project pipeline. 

**Scrap supply** is forecast to post a 2% rise this year, well below our previous estimate, mainly as a result of the limited response from developing countries despite a massive increase in gold prices over the s

ummer. Nevertheless, further price gains, greater distress selling, the emergence of withheld supplies and a belief among a growing number that the price could be cresting should generate a new record for scrap supply in 2012. Thereafter, scrap is set to enter a downward trajectory, broadly in line with price developments and a reduction in distress selling as previously unsettled economies achieve a sounder footing. Given a major lift in our price forecast, it is not surprising that the 2012 and 2013 figures have been revised upward. Another major change on the supply side since our August report is that we expect a return to **net producer hedging** from this year onwards (two years earlier than previously forecast), although volumes should be limited in 2011 and 2012, and would be primarily project related. As the price starts to weaken from 2013 onwards, we expect producers to start cautious hedging to protect revenues, and for this momentum to build in 2014. However, it should be stressed that investor and management aversion towards the practice of hedging has not really changed and, while we are forecasting a return to hedging, by no means will forecast net volumes reach the levels seen in the 1990s. Moving to demand, despite a marked rise in prices this year, the fall in **jewellery demand** is likely to be limited to 2%, thanks to resilient demand in India and China. Moving to 2012, jewellery consumption is forecast to weaken further. To a large extent, this is due to a combination of higher prices and a still challenging world economy, with China the only country to post positive growth. While demand is set to recover in 2013, output will not return to its pre-crisis level until 2014. Since the August report, global gold jewellery consumption has been marked lower, a direct response to the now far higher price forecast and less positive economic outlook. **Other fabrication** is set to rise further next year, on the back of higher electronics and coin offtake. Thereafter, while the former will continue to grow, it will not be sufficient to offset losses in the latter, leaving the overall figure posting a combined 8% drop in the final two years of the forecast. **Net official sector purchases** are forecast to rise by some 380 tonnes in 2011 and then stay elevated in the following two years. It is of note that our forecast has been revised up considerably, reflecting growing concerns over all major currencies particular following the worsening sovereign debt crisis over the last couple of months. Under our **Base Case** , we expect a slowdown in world GDP growth this and next year. This is mainly driven by persistent sovereign debt crises, fiscal policy tightening and a slowdown in industrial production in major advanced economies. Although developing world countries continue to expand, global growth is likely to moderate due to tight monetary policies in a number of countries and downward pressure on external demand stemming from economic and financial problems in industrialised nations. However, we expect global growth to improve gradually over the final two years of our forecast, which is mainly driven by emerging markets. We view this as the most likely scenario with a 45% probability. Our more bullish **Scenario B,** with a 40% probability, predicts a global economic recovery with higher growth rates in the major advanced and developing countries over the forecast period. Under this scenario, we assume that the US government and the Federal Reserve continue to implement loose fiscal and monetary policies. As a consequence, we expect negative real interest rates and rising inflation, with the latter reaching an annual average of 5.8% in 2014. Moreover, the US dollar weakens under this scenario.
